deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. The page sits in the 'Fragmenta ex Adversariis' (Opera Postuma, 1862). The first paragraph finishes a write-up of Lagrange's proof (1770, recorded here by Lexell/Krafft). The rest of the page begins Euler's own proof ('demonstratio mea') of the key lemma for Lagrange's four-square theorem: a prime dividing a sum of four squares is itself a sum of four squares.

(1) END OF LAGRANGE'S DESCENT. The previous page showed the following. Suppose Aa = p^2+q^2+r^2+s^2 with gcd(p^2+q^2, a) = 1. Then one can construct a' = (1+alpha^2+beta^2)/a with Aa' also a sum of four squares, and a' < a/2 + 1/a < a. This page concludes: iterate a > a' > a'' > ... to reach A·1. Hence A is a sum of four squares.

The theorem stated is: if A divides a sum of four squares whose roots have no common factor, then A is a sum of four squares. Equivalently, every divisor of such a sum is such a sum.

(2) EULER, LEMMA I. Let gcd(N,n) = 1. Then every integer A can be written A = Nx + ny (Bezout), and one may take |x| < n/2.
- From one representation A = Nf + ng one gets A = N(f - lambda n) + n(g + lambda N).
- Choose lambda so that 0 <= f - lambda n < n.
- If this residue still exceeds n/2, subtract n once more; the result has absolute value < n/2.
- Signs are irrelevant.
- Modern form: x is the least absolute residue of A·N^{-1} mod n, so |x| <= n/2.

(3) LEMMA II. This is Euler's four-square identity. With
- A = a alpha + b beta + c gamma + d delta,
- B = a beta - b alpha - c delta + d gamma,
- C = a gamma + b delta - c alpha - d beta,
- D = a delta - b gamma + c beta - d alpha,

the identity reads (a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2)(alpha^2+beta^2+gamma^2+delta^2) = A^2+B^2+C^2+D^2. Euler's justification: all doubled cross products cancel in pairs (I verified each of the 12 cross monomials), and each Latin square meets each Greek square exactly once.

(4) THEOREM. If a prime N divides P^2+Q^2+R^2+S^2, then N is a sum of four squares.

Proof as on this page:
- Replace P by P - lambda N (and similarly Q, R, S); divisibility by N is preserved. If a residue exceeds N/2, use N - P. This gives roots p, q, r, s with |.| < N/2.
- So Nn = p^2+q^2+r^2+s^2 < N^2, hence n < N.
- Since N is prime and 1 <= n < N, gcd(N,n) = 1 [my remark: needed for Lemma I]. Lemma I then gives p = Na + n alpha, q = Nb + n beta, r = Nc + n gamma, s = Nd + n delta, with |a|, |b|, |c|, |d| < n/2.
- Expanding: Nn = N^2(a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2) + 2Nn(a alpha + b beta + c gamma + d delta) + n^2(alpha^2+beta^2+gamma^2+delta^2). The middle bracket is the A of Lemma II.
- The last two terms and the left side are divisible by n. So n | N^2(a^2+...+d^2), and since gcd(n,N) = 1, n | a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2.

The page ends with 'Ponatur ergo'. The next page sets a^2+...+d^2 = n n' with n' < n, divides by n, multiplies by n', and uses Lemma II to get N n' = (N n' + A)^2 + B^2 + C^2 + D^2. Descent on n then reaches N·1.

This is the descent now standard in textbooks, e.g. Hardy–Wright Thm 369 style, where 'm0 p = sum of four squares' gives 'm1 p' with m1 < m0.
errors: Theorem statement on this page omits the hypothesis that P, Q, R, S are not all divisible by N. If they all are, the reduced p, q, r, s are all 0 and n = 0, so the argument collapses. The 'alia demonstratio' on the next page adds 'quae singula seorsim per eum non sint divisibilia'.

Lemma I claims strict |x| < n/2, which fails when n is even and the residue equals n/2. The correct bound is |x| <= n/2. In the worked example N=7, n=2 one is forced to take |a| = 1 = n/2. Consequently a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2 <= n^2 rather than < n^2. The next page's conclusion n' < n then needs an extra argument for the equality case (all |a_i| = n/2), which Euler does not give. Modern proofs handle this case separately, e.g. by first making n odd.
Similarly |p| <= N/2 gives only p^2+q^2+r^2+s^2 <= N^2. Strictness (needed for n < N) holds because N is an odd prime; N = 2 is trivial. This is unstated.
Wording slip in Lemma I: 'tum f - n certe minus erit' should refer to the reduced residue (f - lambda n) - n, not f - n.
Lagrange part: the descent Aa -> Aa' needs the coprimality hypothesis (gcd(p'^2+q'^2, a') = 1) to persist at each step. This is not checked in the text.
Notational clash: the letter A denotes both an arbitrary integer (Lemma I) and the bilinear form a alpha + ... (Lemma II/proof). This is harmless.

results.what: Euler's four-square identity (product of two sums of four squares is a sum of four squares), with explicit bilinear forms A, B, C, D
results.usually_credited_to: Euler, letter to Goldbach 4 May 1748; published E242 (1750s)

results.what: Lemma I: A = Nx + ny with |x| <= n/2 when gcd(N,n) = 1
Descent proof that a prime p dividing a sum of four squares is a sum of four squares, via writing p_i = N a_i + n alpha_i and obtaining N n' = (N n' + A)^2 + B^2 + C^2 + D^2 with n' < n
results.modern_name: Euler's descent step in the proof of Lagrange's four-square theorem (textbook 'm0 -> m1' descent)
results.usually_credited_to: Euler, 'Novae demonstrationes circa resolutionem numerorum in quadrata' (E445, Acta Erud. 1773 / 1772); earlier, different descent in E242

results.what: Report of Lagrange's proof (Aa -> Aa' with a' < a/2 + 1/a)

deep.surprise_reason: The material is exactly Euler's published 1772/73 simplification (E445) of the four-square theorem, plus his 1748 identity and a write-up of Lagrange's 1770 proof. All of this is well known and attributed to Euler. The only point of interest is the small rigor gap at |a| = n/2.
